newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia extradition bill remains intact but weak.
newsitem.headline: Colombia extradition bill remains intact but weak.

text.p: The Colombian government's bid to lift a six-year-old ban on the extradition of drug traffickers and other criminals remained intact but seriously weakened after a rocky congressional debate on Tuesday.

The 32-member committee of Congress' lower house left the question of whether extradition would be applied retroactively hanging in the balance after removing key wording from the original government proposal, which many critics said was already so watered down as to be useless.
Senior government ministers, who spent much of the day feverishly lobbying lawmakers, were upbeat about the outcome and said the legislation could be beefed up in future congressional debates.

The Chamber of Representatives committee voted clause by clause on the bill at the end of a grueling 14-hour debate. The proposal must still survive a vote in the plenary session of the Chamber on June 19 and four further votes in a fresh session of Congress that begins mid-July if it is to make its way on to the statute books.

"I'm a friend of the government and so I didn't vote in favour of extradition because the first one to be extradited would be President Ernesto Samper," said lawmaker Roberto Herrera, a member of the ruling Liberal Party.

Herrera was referring to the political scandal that has dogged Samper's administration, sparked by allegations that he funded his 1994 election campaign with multi-million dollar donations from the notorious Cali drug cartel.
Samper was cleared of any wrongdoing after a congressional inquiry last year but the United States withdrew his U.S. entry visa citing his "known ties to drug traffickers".

If the bill survives in its present form it would forbid extradition if alleged criminals surrender to the Colombian authorities or if they face tougher penalties abroad than they would under the notoriously lenient Colombian justice system.

The Chamber removed all reference as to whether extradition could be applied retroactively or simply from the moment the bill became law -- effectively leaving such a decision to a future session of Congress.

Justice Minister Almabeatriz Rengifo said the issue of retroactivity had been "eliminated" from the bill but said the government's efforts to lift the 1991 ban on extraditing Colombian nationals was still on track.

Interior Minister Carlos Holmes Trujillo, who took office earlier in the day, said after the vote: "This reestablishes the extradition of Colombians but the question of when it would come into effect remains open."

U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration has pushed hard for the re-establishment of extradition and insisted the measure should be retroactive to allow cartel leaders already behind bars in Colombia to be sent for trial in U.S. courts.
Many lawmakers in Tuesday's debate argued that a vote in favour of reintroducing extradition was tantamount to kowtowing to the United States and sacrificing national sovereignty.

Extradition was banned in 1991 after Pablo Escobar, the late kingpin of the Medellin cartel, unleashed a savage war against the state under the slogan "We prefer a tomb in Colombia than a cell in the United States".
